verdicts.evidence:
"The proposal itself gets converted to a concern first and admitted only through three
questions: which uncovered concern it serves, which judgment would differ with it
present, and whether an existing item already measures the same thing — if no judgment
changes, it is parked, not added. Once every concern has an item and no overlap remains
unmerged, I'd record the chosen operating points ... and freeze the set, so future
adjustments mean adding or merging a concern rather than editing item count directly."
This adds the rubric's explicit park-if-no-judgment-changes and freeze-once-derived
conditions, which the blind answer (concern-first, merge, no direct edits) implied but
never stated; no forbidden item (local-merits admission, double-counting, direct
add/delete fixes) appears in the injected answer.

"a confirmation nobody in this context can answer is effectively a block, so I'd lower
it or scope it with a documented bypass (a non-interactive flag, or narrowing the
confirm to the risky subset such as the one key whose overwrite forces re-auth). Then
I'd run the deletion test on the other three gates — name the concrete failure and
reachable actor each catches ... and downgrade or drop any gate with no named failure
— and finally walk one failure alone to confirm a single rejected write doesn't void
the whole scripted run." The blind answer walked the path and fixed the confirmation
but kept the other three checks "fully intact" with no named-failure justification and
no rung calibration or failure attribution; the injected answer adds all of these
rubric elements and triggers no forbidden item.
